book.title: A Dictionary of English and Welsh Surnames, with Special American Instances
book.author: Charles Wareing Bardsley

headwords.meaning: the son of Aaron
headwords.author_comment: A Jewish surname settled in England. I have not met with a single English Aaron in mediaeval times.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam (Welsh ap- or ab-Adam)
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Bethell, Bloyd, Breeze, &c.

headwords.meaning: (1) at the Abbey, from residence thereby; (2) from the ecclesiastical title
headwords.author_comment: All the evidence is in favour of this view except in one instance.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abraham, or Abell, from the nick. Abb, with double dim. Abb-in-et
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Robinet and Colinet.

headwords.meaning: variant of Abbs
headwords.author_comment: V. Abbs, of which, no doubt, it is a variant.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Abraham, from the nick. Abb, and dim. Abb-ot; (2) the Abbot, an official title or nickname
headwords.author_comment: It is all but certain that the majority of our Abbotts, although bearing a conventual title, are thus descended [from Abraham]. Abraham was a favourite name in the 13th century. Abel was also popular, and may have shared the parentage.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abraham or Abel, from nick. Abb or Abbie
headwords.author_comment: This was a familiar Norfolk surname as Abbys or Abbes. To-day it is familiar in the same county as Abbs.

headwords.meaning: of the Abdy; query, an old form of 'Abbey' (?)
headwords.author_comment: Lower says: 'Abdy, an estate in Yorkshire, where the family anciently resided.' This is corroborated by the following entries. All these [1379 entries] were living at Brampton-juxta-Wath. The 'del' is interesting.

headwords.meaning: at the Beck-head, from residence at the head or source of the beck
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Birkett, originally Birk-head, or Birkenhead, the head of the birch-trees. Birkett is a Cumberland surname. Birkenhead, co. Chester, is but a variant, being the adjectival form; v. Beck. Cf. Roger a'Hulle (co. Oxf., 1273. A.), i.e. Roger at the Hill.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abel
headwords.author_comment: Much more popular in mediaeval society than in that of the 19th century. Among the peasantry, however, Abel still receives a certain amount of attention as a font-name.
headwords.modern_distribution: Boston (U.S.), 58, 10, 2, 0, 0; London, 7, 8, 1, 1, 0; MDB. (N. Rid. Yorkshire), Able 1

headwords.meaning: Ab-Ithel (Welsh), i.e. the son of Ithel
headwords.author_comment: v. Bethell, and cf. Abadam.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abel, from dim. Abel-ot
headwords.author_comment: A feminine form occurs in the Hundred Rolls; v. infra.

headwords.meaning: doubtless a corruption of Applethwaite, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Hebblewhite.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abel, from the dim. Abel-in
headwords.author_comment: v. Aplin (2).

headwords.headword: Abraham, Abrahams, Abrahamson, Abram, Abrams, Abramson
headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Abraham; (2) of Abram, a township in the parish of Wigan, Lancashire
headwords.author_comment: (1) A popular font-name in the 13th century; v. Abbot. In the Fen district especially the entries are common. The instances in the Hundred Rolls are all but entirely confined to the Fen counties. A glance at the London Directory will show that in general Abraham represents the old English stock, and Abrahams the more modern Jewish. This is proved by comparing the personal or Christian names prefixed to the instances; cf. Solomon and Salmon. (2) Abram was originally written Adburgham. The Lancashire Abram and Abraham spring from this place.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abrahee, presumably a form of Abraham
the son of Absolom
headwords.author_comment: A fairly popular font-name in the 13th century, and not confined to the Jews. 'Now was ther of that chirche a parish clerk, The which that was ycleped Absolon.' Chaucer, C. T. 3312.

headwords.meaning: the son of Abraham; v. Abbs
at the burn, corrupted to Aburn
headwords.author_comment: Cf. A'Becket, A'Wood, &c.

headwords.meaning: see Cator (a buyer of victuals)
headwords.author_comment: Chaucer says of the manciple who was so 'wise in buying of victuals,' that of him 'Achatours mighten take ensample.'

headwords.meaning: the son of Achard
headwords.author_comment: v. Hatchard.

headwords.meaning: see Atkirk
the Acreman: a ploughman, a husbandman, a tiller of the soil
headwords.author_comment: 'both prestis and knightis mosten bicome acremen and heerdis,' 1389: Hist. Eng. Dic. 'The foules up, and song on bough, And acremen yede to the plough.' Lay le Freine, 176 (Halliwell). Akermann is of German birth.

headwords.meaning: at the Ackley, i.e. the oak-meadow
headwords.author_comment: The exact equivalent of Oakley, q.v.

headwords.meaning: of Acklam, two parishes in co. York, one in the union of Malton, the other in the union of Stockton
of the Ackroyd, i.e. the oak clearing
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Ormerod, Murgatroyd, &c. A well-known Yorkshire surname.
headwords.modern_distribution: West Riding Court Dir., 28, 2, 0, 2, 6; MDB. (W. Riding), 17, 0, 1, 4, 0; Philadelphia, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0

headwords.meaning: of Acland (Ac or Oakland, named from a large grove of oaks; Saxon ac)
headwords.author_comment: 'From the situation of their ancient seat in Lankey, near Barnstaple, co. Devon, which, being in the midst of a large grove of oaks (in Saxon ac), obtained the name of Ac or Oakland. ... They were settled in this place as early as the reign of Henry II.' (Lower, quoting Kimber's Baronetage.)
headwords.modern_distribution: Exeter, 1, 2; MDB. (co. Devon), 3, 2; London, 4, 6; Philadelphia, 0, 2; Boston, 0, 3

headwords.meaning: the son of Alcock (q.v.), corrupted to Accock, which took the imitative form of Haycock
headwords.author_comment: At least it would appear so. If we could find any instances of Halcock representing Henry, we should then be obliged to refer the three last to that personal name.

headwords.meaning: (1) of Acomb, a parish near York; (2) of Acomb, two townships in the union of Hexham, co. Northumberland
variant of Acock
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Glasscock for Glasscott.

headwords.meaning: of the Acre, or Acres, from residence beside the field or fields called the Acre or Acres
of Acton, i.e. the farmstead among the oaks
headwords.author_comment: There are in England no less than sixteen parishes, hamlets, townships, &c., called Acton.

headwords.meaning: of Ackworth, a parish near Wakefield, co. York
the son of Adam
headwords.author_comment: Almost the prime favourite as a font-name in the 13th century; v. Addis, Adcock, Atkins, Atkinson, Addyman, &c. Adams is remarkably well represented in the United States. A single glance at the Index to Hotten's Lists of Emigrants will suffice to show that many Adams, Addams, Adamsons, or Addamsons were among the early settlers.

headwords.meaning: of Adamthwaite (i.e. the clearing of Adam the first settler, probably in the 12th century), a small hamlet in Ravenstonedale, co. Westm.
headwords.author_comment: v. Thwaites.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Ade with suffix -cock
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Wilcock, Jeffcock, Watcock, &c.; v. Addis with Atcock; cf. Atkins for Adkins.

headwords.meaning: of Atherley, a parish in co. Salop, pronounced Adderley
the son of Adam, from an early dim. (?)
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Adnett and Adnitt, q.v.

headwords.headword: Addis, Addison, Adds, Addy, Ade, Ades, Adey, Adie, Ady, Addey, Aday, Adee
headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Ad, Ade, or Addy
headwords.author_comment: All are reminders of the wonderful popularity of Adam in the north of England, if not in the south; cf. Adcock and Adkin, q.v. A common entry in the Hundred Rolls [of the 'fil. Ade' form]. With the variant Adice cf. Ellice for Ellis, or Bevance for Bevans.

headwords.meaning: the servant or knave of Addy, i.e. Adam
headwords.author_comment: v. Addy and Addison. This is decidedly interesting. It is one of the chief witnesses to-day of the existence of the class of surnames to which it belongs. As a matter of course its home is in Yorkshire; cf. Mathewman, Peterman, Perryman, Jackman, Bartleman, &c. In the following entries, although Ade (i.e. Addy) is given as the nick. of Adam, the entry is unfortunately in Latin. In English it would have read Thomas and Johannes Addyman. We are more fortunate in a further instance, where the English form is given.

headwords.meaning: see Addis

headwords.headword: Adkin, Adkins, Adkinson, Atkin, Atkins, Atkinson, Atkyns, Adkisson
headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Addy, dim. Adkin, sharpened to Atkin
headwords.author_comment: There is no need of course to prove this, but it is interesting to note the following: 'Adam le Fullere,' a citizen of London, is twice referred to as Adekin le Fullere (1273, Hundred Rolls, i. 426). Six centuries ago Adam probably ranked as second or third favourite among boys' names throughout England. In the north it attained a most remarkable pre-eminence. Four Adams are mentioned in the revenues of Conishead Priory, A.D. 1256 (West's Furness, pp. 192, 195). No fewer than six Adams figure as benefactors of Furness Abbey, circa 1290 (ibid.). The everyday form was Adekin, then Adkin, and finally Atkin (see Addison). The following come together [Johannes Attekyson and Alicia soror Adekynson].

headwords.meaning: see Adnam
the son of Adelard or Athelard
headwords.author_comment: v. Allard. Adelhard was a cousin of Charlemagne, and Abbot of Corbie. (Yonge, ii. 399.)

headwords.meaning: the son of Adeline, alias Atheline
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Athelard and Adlard.

headwords.meaning: of Addingham; parishes in co. Cumberland and W. Rid. Yorkshire
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Swetnam and Swetman for Swettenham, or Debnam and Deadman for Debenham, or Putnam and Putman for Puttenham. Adlam is a further and natural variant; cf. bannister for baluster. With Adnum, cf. Barnum for Barnham.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Addy, dim. Add-in, second dim. Add-in-et
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Addinson, q.v. Adin or Addin was evidently the O.F. equivalent of Adkin, the customary English form; v. Atkins and Atkinson.

headwords.meaning: local origin (?) - uncertain
the son of Adrian
headwords.author_comment: The form Adrain is an old one. The sheriff, John Adrian, entered below, is recorded as John Adrain: A. i. p. 403.

headwords.meaning: of Adshead, some spot in the neighbourhood of Prestbury, co. Chester
headwords.author_comment: Prestbury church register teems with entries relating to the family. The surname has crossed the Atlantic.

headwords.meaning: of Auchinleck, N.B. (North Britain, i.e. Scotland)
headwords.author_comment: 'A singular contraction of the surname Auchinleck, borne by an ancient family "of that ilk" in Ayrshire. Sir Edmund Affleck, created baronet in 1782, was sixth in descent from Sir John Auchinleck, son of Gilbert A. of Auchinleck': Lower, Pat. Brit., p. 3.

headwords.meaning: the son of Agar, or Ager
headwords.author_comment: Probably a form of Algar, a Domesday personal name, and very popular for several centuries; v. Algar.

headwords.meaning: see Haggard
headwords.author_comment: Arthur Agard, a distinguished antiquary, was descended of an old Derbyshire family. He was born in 1540, and died in 1615. He was one of the original members of the Society of Antiquaries, and was buried in Westminster Abbey. (Dict. Nat. Biog. i. 173, and Stanley's Westminster Abbey, p. 443.) Haggard is the usual form of this patronymic.

headwords.meaning: the son of Agace; a form of Agatha
(1) at the gate, from residence thereby; (2) the son of Agnes, from the nick. Agg, dim. Agot
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Atwood, Bywater, &c.

headwords.meaning: the son of Agnes, from the nick. Agg
headwords.author_comment: Aggie is still the favourite north English nick.

headwords.meaning: a corruption of Acland, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Ackland, Acland, and Agland are all found indifferently in co. Devon, the home of the name; v. Devon Directory; cf. the Lancashire Ogden for Oakden.

headwords.meaning: of Aglionby, a township in the parish of Warwick, three miles from Carlisle, co. Cumb.
a needler, a maker of needles (O.F. aguille, a needle)
headwords.author_comment: 'A silver needle forth I drew / Out of an aguiler quaint ynow.' Chaucer, Rom. Rose, 98. O.F. aguille, a needle.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam, from the nick. Ade and dim. Adkin
headwords.author_comment: The Scotch form of Atkin, q.v., was Aitkin. This was further corrupted to Aiken and Aikin.

headwords.meaning: see Askew
of Annesley, a parish in co. Notts, near Nottingham
headwords.author_comment: But there is probably a north English local origin also. There is also Ansley, a parish in co. Warwick.

headwords.meaning: of Ainsworth, a chapelry in the parish of Middleton, co. Lanc., formerly Aynesworth
of Airey
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the spot, but the family arose in co. Cumberland or Westmoreland. Almost every instance can be traced back to one or other county.

headwords.meaning: (?) the son of Auskettle, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Probably a modified form. On the other hand it may be local, with the suffix -gill, so common to the narrow gorges of the northern counties.

headwords.meaning: of Aislaby, (1) a township in the parish of Egglescliffe, co. Durh.; (2) a chapelry in the parish of Whitby, N.R. Yorks, formerly Aslakeby (v. Aslac); hence 'the dwelling of Aslac,' the first settler
headwords.author_comment: 'Aislabie, one of the oldest names in the county of Durham, from Aislaby, a parish on the river Tees, on the banks of which the family still reside. In old documents it is written Ashlackby, and in about fifty other modes' (Lower).

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Archibald (?), from the nick. Archie, a Scotch Border favourite; t intrusive, as in Ritchie, from same district; (2) the son of Adkin, q.v.: a Border form of the great north English surname Atkinson
headwords.author_comment: (1) t intrusive, as in Ritchie, from same district, q.v. (2) A Border form of the great north English surname Atkinson. This is the true source of the majority of our Aitchesons, &c. Atshison = Atkinson: Dickinson's Glossary of the Words and Phrases of Cumberland, p. 4.

headwords.meaning: the son of Adam; the Scotch Border form of Atkin, q.v.
a variant of Hazlewood, q.v.
at the oak-head (from residence thereby), the top or furthest reach of the oak-trees
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Birk-head, now Birkett; and v. Akenhead for further instances.

headwords.meaning: v. Akenside
headwords.author_comment: Lower says, 'Akenhead: Akenside - doubtless local; from Aiken, an early proprietor.' This latter statement is wholly incorrect.

headwords.meaning: of Akenside, i.e. the side of the clump of oak-trees; A.S. acen; cf. Beechen, Linden, Birchen, with the adjectival suffix -en
headwords.author_comment: The place, whether a manor or mere farmstead, is distinctly set down in the list of landed proprietors in Hodgson's Hist. of Northumberland (iv. 268). Akenside, the poet, it will be remembered, was born at Newcastle-on-Tyne in 1721. His parentage and descent, therefore, were strictly local, and his 'forbears' had wandered but a few miles from their original home; cf. Thomas Carlyle and the city Carlisle (v. Carlisle). -side is a common suffix of north English local names, used in the same sense as lake-side, pit-side; cf. Fawcett or Garside, q.v. Also, cf. Adam de Birkinside, 1322: E. and F., co. Cumb. p. 165. Akenhead, i.e. at the head of the oak-trees, corresponds with Birkenhead, Birkett, and Beckett, q.v.

headwords.meaning: of Acaster, two parishes of this name near York
headwords.author_comment: This surname has crossed from Yorkshire into Furness, Lancashire.

headwords.meaning: the Arbalester, i.e. cross-bowman; O.F. arbalestier; v. H.E.D.
headwords.author_comment: Illustrated by verses from Robert of Gloucester ('Spearmen anote, and bowemen, and also arblasters') and Chaucer, Rom. Rose, 4196 ('Of arblasters great plentie were').

headwords.meaning: (1) de Albini, not the Scotch Albany; (2) the son of Alban, popularly Albany
headwords.author_comment: (1) 'William de Albini attended William the Conqueror. Wace mentions him as "the butler d'Aubignie"' (Lower). Hence the Earls of Arundel. (2) This form has survived in some districts till to-day.

headwords.meaning: the son of Albert, from Ethelbert or Adelbert; German Albrecht
headwords.author_comment: v. also Allbright for further instances. The Albrechts of the London Dir. are all of late German immigration. Also the Albrechts of Philadelphia.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Albray, probably Aubrey; (2) of Aldbury, a parish in co. Hertfordshire, three miles from Tring
headwords.author_comment: v. Albury for other instances.

headwords.meaning: the son of Albin or Alban; pet form Albany, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: Earlier still, in 1269, we find one Albin de Dereby forbidden to dwell within the precincts of London city: WWW. p. 125. For other examples see next article.

headwords.meaning: the son of Albin, or Alban; v. Albin
headwords.author_comment: The following entry [1790, Jane Alberson] has probably no connexion with Alberston. With this variant cf. Patterson for Pattinson.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alban; v. Allbon
of Albury, or Aldborough, parishes in cos. Norfolk, Suffolk, York (W.R.), York (E.R.), and Hertford
headwords.author_comment: v. Eldborough.

headwords.meaning: the son of Albot, probably a popular form of Albrecht; v. Albert
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 1, 0; West Riding Court Dir., 0, 2; Philadelphia, 0, 1

headwords.meaning: the son of Allen, from the pet form Allicock or Allcock; v. Cock, and cf. Wilcock, Jeffcock, Simcock
headwords.author_comment: 'The same holds one messuage which formerly belonged to Matilda Alcoke, doghtyr.' 'The same holds one tenement which formerly belonged to Alcoke of Hynganderode': Rental of Halifax (1439), Cotton MSS. Vespasian; F. 15, Brit. Mus. Mr. Lower says this name is a dim. of Hal, the nick. of Henry. The evidence is against this view; v. Allkin. There is clear proof that the original form was Alycock, and that this was abbreviated to Al-cock. Allen would readily take the nick. Ally or Aly, and the suffix -cock was added as a matter of course. The important point is to remember the enormous popularity of Allen in the 13th and 14th centuries, and the absolute certainty that both nick. and pet forms would be in everyday use.

headwords.meaning: of Aldham, q.v.
the son of Aldwin; i.e. Aylwin, with intrusive d
headwords.author_comment: 'This town (Shelton, co. Norf.) in the Confessor's time belonged to Bishop Stigand, and was held of him by Aldwin, or Alwin': FF. v. 263. The surname was common in the 13th century, but, like every other of the numerous compounds of -win, settled into -en, -in, and -ing; cf. Golden, Goldin, Goulding. Audenshaw, a division of Ashton-under-Lyne, was originally Aldwinshaigh, i.e. the wood of Aldwin.

headwords.meaning: at the alder-tree; from residence thereby
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Ash, Nash, Birch, Rowntree, &c. The plural is found in the two entries following [Thomas and Henry in the Alren]. 'Aldren = elders': Halliwell. Thus the d in Alder is excrescent.

headwords.meaning: the alderman, probably used sometimes personally
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Bateman, Tiddyman, &c.

headwords.meaning: of Aldersey, a township in the parish of Coddington, near Chester
headwords.author_comment: This is settled beyond controversy by the following entries. The grandfather of Anne and Margaret Aldersey was 'John Aldersey, of Aldersey, co. Chester,' who married Anne Low, sister of Sir Thomas Low, alderman of London. Their father was Samuel Aldersey, of London, haberdasher: v. Visitation of London, 1633-4, p. 8.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aldus (v. Aldhous), a once familiar personal name
headwords.author_comment: Aldus-son would soon settle down into Alderson.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 11; West Rid. Court Dir., 7; Philadelphia, 3

headwords.meaning: of Aldham, probably an early form of Oldham, co. Lanc., on the borders of Yorkshire
headwords.author_comment: There are, however, parishes of this name in cos. Essex and Suffolk.

headwords.headword: Aldhouse, Aldhous, Aldis, Aldous, Aldus, Alldiss
headwords.meaning: the son of Aldus
headwords.author_comment: Not local, as several of its corrupted forms would seem to prove. These are simply imitative. The documentary proofs are extremely strong. Norfolk has been a long-established home for this name, both in its fontal and patronymic character.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aldith, an early form of Edith (?)
the son of Aldred
headwords.author_comment: This personal name died out soon after the surname epoch, and instances of its occurrence as a fontal name are scarce.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alderich
headwords.author_comment: Although wearing a local guise, it is easy to see that Aldridge belongs to the baptismal class.

headwords.meaning: of Aldwinkle, a parish three miles from Thrapston, co. Northampton
of Aldworth, a parish in co. Berks, near Wantage
the alefounder, an inspector appointed by the Court Leet to assize and supervise the brewing of malt liquor
headwords.author_comment: Another term for this office was ale-conner. A poem of James I's reign says-'A nose he had that gan show, What liquor he loved I trow; For he had before long seven years Been of the towne the ale-conner.' A confirmation by John, Abbot of Cockerham, Lancashire, 1 Ric. III, says, in regulating the price of beer, 'Yai sall gyf Ale-fwnders a fwnding galon or else a taste of ylke vessell,' &c.; Baines' Lanc. ii. 588. This word is neither in Halliwell nor in the Hist. Eng. Dictionary; cf. 'fondyn, or asayyn-attempto,' Prompt. Parv. p. 169. Way adds in a note: 'A.S. fandian, tentare.' Lower quotes from the Norfolk Chronicle, Aug. 19, 1854, a Court Leet of the Borough of New Buckenham at which 'the sub-bailiff, affiers, searchers, and sealers of leather, examiners of fish and flesh, alefounders, inspectors of weights and measures, and a pinder were appointed': Patr. Brit. p. 5. Again Lower quotes from Three Early Metr. Rom. (Camden Soc.), p. xxxviii: 'In the records of the manor of Hale in the xvth cent. one Thomas Layet is mentioned as being fined ... for having concealed the founding pot (quia concelavit le fowundynge pot), 3d.' Evidently the official term as well as the surname were in existence in Norfolk till a very recent period.

headwords.meaning: the ale-tunner, one who filled tuns or casks with ale
headwords.author_comment: v. Turner and Tunneler.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alexander
headwords.author_comment: v. Saunders. This personal name is common to all Europe, and in England was an early favourite. Stories of prodigious achievements, many of them miraculous, caused it to be immensely admired. Miss Yonge (i. 199-202) quotes Chaucer as saying-'Alisaundres storie is commune, That everie wight that hath discrecion Hath herde somewhat.' 'Alysaunder, propyr name Alexander': Prompt. Parv.

headwords.meaning: of Alford; parishes in cos. Linc. and Somerset, and no doubt smaller spots in various counties, as meaning 'the old ford'
headwords.author_comment: For the form Alforth, v. Forth.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alfred, or Alured
headwords.author_comment: This latter form is still found as a surname, although Alfred has long been the accepted orthography of the fontal name. It is curious that Alfred has so few representatives in the directories. Where Allen occupies columns, Alfred occupies lines.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alfrey, i.e. Alfred
headwords.author_comment: Alfried, Alfred, Alfrey; cf. Godfrey, Godfried, Humfrey, Humfreid: Yonge, i. pp. lxviii and lxxviii.

headwords.meaning: the son of Algar, or Alfgar
headwords.author_comment: In Domesday commonly found as Algar. It is also met with alone without surname attached in the Hundred Rolls, ii. 472. This surname is a familiar one as Algar in co. Norfolk. It is early found there both as a personal and a surname. Algar, although forgotten now, was evidently popular in its day and generation; cf. the place-name Algersthorp, co. Norf.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Alice; (2) the son of Alice, from the popular dim. Alison; (3) the son of Allen, corrupted from Allenson
headwords.author_comment: (2) cf. Marion from Mary, Gibbon from Gib (i.e. Gilbert), Beaton from Beatrice, &c. 'This Alison answered: Who is there That knocketh so?' Chaucer, C. T. 3788. (3) Such a corruption was bound to take place; cf. Pattinson and Pattison. There can be no doubt many of our Allisons are traceable to this source. For early instances, v. Allenson. Allison has ramified very strongly in the United States.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 2, 15; West Rid. Court Dir., 0, 6; Philadelphia, 0, 86

headwords.meaning: of Altcar, a village six miles from Ormskirk, co. Lancaster
headwords.author_comment: This surname is rarely found outside the county. Its origin is easily proved by the following instances.

headwords.meaning: see Allkins
see Allman; cf. Lallimand
the son of Alard, abbreviated from Adelard
headwords.author_comment: v. Adlard.

headwords.meaning: of Allardyce, an estate in the parish of Arbuthnot, co. Kincardine, N.B.
the son of Elliot, q.v., the dim. of Ellis
see Allvey, Alloway
headwords.author_comment: This is a natural variant, the intrusive a being euphonic; cf. Greenaway, Hathaway, Ottaway, &c.

headwords.meaning: variant of Alabaster
headwords.author_comment: An American variant.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alban, patr. Albans
headwords.author_comment: v. Albinson. In the register of the parish church, Bolingbroke, Albans in the 17th century is represented by Allbones in the 19th; v. Allibone, Alban, and Albany. 'Stol'n from mine host of S. Albones': Falstaff, 1 Hen. IV, iv. 2.

headwords.meaning: the son of Ailbrit; in Domesday Ailbriht
headwords.author_comment: Albrecht is a German immigrant of much later date. Allbright is English. Albert, again, is ancient and modern. For other instances, v. Albert.

headwords.meaning: variant of Albutt
(1) the son of Alcuin (v. Yonge, ii. 350), corrupted to Oldcorn in north England; (2) of Alchorne, a manor in the parish of Rotherfield, co. Sussex, where the family lived in the 14th century
headwords.author_comment: I have one representative in my parish (Ulverston). I place all these surnames together because it is impossible to separate them. No doubt both (2) and (1) have assimilated. In a general way Alchorn represents the local, and Alcorn the personal surname. (2) Some of their descendants, still resident in that parish, have, within a generation or two, corrupted their name to Allcorn (Lower).

headwords.meaning: see Holdcroft
the son of Aldy, a popular form of Aldwin, or Aldred, or Aldrich, or Aldus, or some other of the once popular compounds of Ald
headwords.author_comment: But the probable ancestor was Aldwin, which was early modified into Aldwy; v. Allvey.

headwords.headword: Allen, Alleine, Alleyne, Allan, Allin, Alland
headwords.meaning: the son of Alan, or Allen, or Aleyn (Yonge, i. 396-7)
headwords.author_comment: 'Aleyne, propyr name, Alanus': Prompt. Parv. 'Forth goth Alein, the clerk, and also John.'—Chaucer, C. T. 4015. (The d in Alland is an excrescence as in Simmonds.) One of our most popular names while surnames were becoming hereditary; said to have come into England with Alan Fergéant, Count of Brittany, a companion of the Conqueror, and first Earl of Richmond, co. York. Very soon common to north England and the Scottish border. The founder of Dulwich Coll., 1619, was Edward Allen, or Alleyne. Derivatives, Allcock, Allkins, Allnutt, and perhaps Allatt, q.v. Possibly an abbrev. of Alinot; v. Allnutt.

headwords.meaning: doubtless a modification of Aglionby, q.v.
headwords.author_comment: The surname is found in Cumberland, and the full title was cumbrous.

headwords.meaning: (1) the son of Allen, q.v.; (2) de Alençon, in Normandy
headwords.author_comment: (2) Probably in some cases this is the true solution.

headwords.meaning: of Allerton, a parish five miles from Knaresborough, co. York; also a township in the parish of Childwall, near Liverpool; also a township in the parish of Kippax, W. Rid. York
headwords.author_comment: cf. Northallerton.

headwords.meaning: (1) of the Alley, i.e. from residence in a narrow passage; M.E. aley and alley; (2) probably in some cases Alley, a pet-name for Allen and Alice
headwords.author_comment: The first instance I possess is that of a foundling, found in an alley. But the name was an older one, of similar but more legitimate descent. The Hundred Rolls instances from Oxford and Cambridge seem very natural, just where we should expect alleys to be found; v. Twitchen. (2) A pet-name for very great favourites, Allen and Alice, q.v.; cf. Charlie, Teddy, &c.

headwords.meaning: see Alfrey
the son of Algod, a forgotten personal name
headwords.author_comment: Allgood, like Thoroughgood and Toogood, seems very complimentary, but it is without doubt a baptismal name, as are they. I see Lower says Algod occurs as a personal name before Domesday (Patr. Brit. p. 6).

headwords.meaning: the son of Alban, or Albon
headwords.author_comment: v. Allbon. The i and a are intrusive for euphony, as in Greenaway, Hathaway, for Greenway and Hathway; cf. Ottaway for Ottway. The d in Allibond is excrescent; cf. provincial gownd for gown, and v. Simmonds. A book on the 'Cure of Consumption' is advertized by the author, Edwin W. Alabone, in the Weekly Pulpit for May 22, 1887. Allaband and Alleborn are American variants.

headwords.meaning: of Allingham, a parish in co. Kent
of Allington, parishes in cos. Dorset, Kent, Wilts, Devon, and Lincoln
the son of Alice
headwords.author_comment: v. Alison (1).

headwords.meaning: variant of Alison
the son of Allen, from the dim. Allikin or Allkin
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Per-kin, Wat-kin, &c. Mr. Lower suggests that it stands for Halkin, the dim. of Henry. This view is defeated by the fact that Alkin has always been without the aspirate, and has always run side by side with its close relation Alcock, q.v. Let it not be forgotten that Allen, as one of the favourite personal names of the 13th and 14th centuries, must have had its popular nick. and pet forms. I have included Allchin and Alchin as variants of Allkin. But v. Allcorn.

headwords.meaning: the Alemaund, i.e. German; or still more locally 'of Alemaigne,' i.e. Germany
headwords.author_comment: Cf. Fr. Lallimond; cf. Fr. D'Almaine. With Almond cf. almond-furnace, i.e. a German furnace (H.E.D.); also under Almain, 'the almond-leape,' a German dance. 'The Almains ben ouer come,' 1314: Guy Warw. 70 (H.E.D.). 'Forth he went into Speyne And after into Almayne.'—ibid. 35. 'Item, the last daie (Nov. 1531) paide in rewarde to a gentleman of Almayne': Privy Purse Exp., Henry VIII, p. 178.

headwords.meaning: variant of Hallmark
the son of Alnot or Alnoth, the A.S. Alnod
headwords.author_comment: As will be seen from the above instances, Alnot or Alnoth remained in use as a personal name till the 16th century.

headwords.meaning: the son of Alot; query, a form of Eliot, with Eliota as fem.
headwords.author_comment: v. Elliot. In the Ulverston Registers, co. Lanc., the forms are Alletson, Aletson, Elatson, Elattson, Elletson, Eletson, all representing the same patronymic Eliotson; v. Alletson in Index of Registers of St. Mary, Ulverston. In any case the surname, with its variants, is of fontal origin.

headwords.meaning: the son of Aldwy
headwords.author_comment: v. Allaway and Allvey, where Alway is clearly identified. From Alway or Allway to Alloway is an easy gradation; cf. Ottaway or Greenaway for Otway and Greenway. Alloway has ramified somewhat strongly in America. But it arose in England. No connexion with local Holloway; v. Allaway.

headwords.meaning: (?) the holy priest (?); A.S. halig, holy, from hal, whole
headwords.author_comment: Whatever the meaning, the following entry refers to the ancestor. Thus -prest (priest) and not -press is the suffix. The surname has always had cos. Cambridge and Hants for its habitat. There need be no anxiety as to the want of an h if Holy-priest be the parent. The Hundred Rolls (1273) in scores of cases ignore the aspirate. The Cockney is not in it, judging by early registers.

headwords.meaning: of Alsop-en-le-dale, a chapelry in the parish of Ashbourne, co. Derby
headwords.author_comment: The corruption 'Allsup' is suggestive of universal pale ale! The reason why Alsop and its variants are common in the United States is because several of the name were among the earliest settlers there.

headwords.meaning: variant of Alfred
the son of Aldwy, a fontal or personal name long ago forgotten in England
headwords.author_comment: It lives to-day in several patronymics. Of some land in Somerton, co. Norfolk, it is said 'the Conqueror had granted this to Alwy de Tetford' (FF. xi. 197).

headwords.meaning: the son of Aldrich
headwords.author_comment: Mr. Lower suggests Awl-wright, a maker of awls. The origin is obvious enough. It is a mere corruption of Alderich (now Aldrich and Aldridge, q.v.), thus: Alderich, Alrick, Alwright; cf. Woolwright for Wulfric (v. Woolrich), and Kenwright for Kendrick. A good example of the intermediate form is found in the following instances.

headwords.meaning: variant of Allman
(?) origin queried by the author
the Alpe, i.e. a bullfinch
headwords.author_comment: 'Alpe, a bryde: ficedula': Prompt. Parv. 'Alpes, fynches, and wodewales': Chaucer, R. R. 658. Alpe has existed as a surname in co. Norfolk for six centuries; cf. Finch, Sparrow, Nightingale, &c.

headwords.meaning: of Alstead
headwords.author_comment: I cannot find the precise locality; but v. Halstead.

headwords.meaning: of Alston, a parish in co. Cumberland; a chapelry in the parish of Ashburton, co. Devon; a township in the parish of Ribchester, co. Lanc., &c. Also Alstone, a hamlet in the suburbs of Cheltenham, and a chapelry in the parish of Overbury, co. Worc.
possibly from the high and low range of voice
headwords.author_comment: But see legal 'alto et basso,' the submission of all differences, high and low, to an adjudicator (Bailey's Dict., 1742).

headwords.meaning: the ambler, one who looked after the amblers in his lord's stables; one who taught horses to amble
headwords.author_comment: Lower says 'le Ambleur, Fr., an officer of the king's stable.' Almost akin to Palfreyman, q.v. This surname has ramified strongly in Yorkshire. 'And mony fat palfray amblant' [i.e. ambling]. King Alisaunder, 3461. 'Upon an ambler esily she sat.' Chaucer, C. T. 471. Among his other duties the ambler broke in horses, i.e. taught them to amble. '1320. Item, pro informatione unius pulli ad ambulandum, 11s. 6d,' i.e. for teaching a colt to amble. Whittaker's Craven, p. 466.
headwords.modern_distribution: London, 5; West Riding Court Dir., 25; Philadelphia, 18

headwords.meaning: the son of Amery
headwords.author_comment: q.v.; cf. Emberson and Embery from Emery. The b is intrusive, as usual after m.
